<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Groundwater resources are vital to ecosystems and livelihoods. Excessive groundwater withdrawals can cause groundwater levels to decline
                    <jats:sup>1–10</jats:sup>
                    , resulting in seawater intrusion
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    , land subsidence
                    <jats:sup>12,13</jats:sup>
                    , streamflow depletion
                    <jats:sup>14–16</jats:sup>
                    and wells running dry
                    <jats:sup>17</jats:sup>
                    . However, the global pace and prevalence of local groundwater declines are poorly constrained, because in situ groundwater levels have not been synthesized at the global scale. Here we analyse in situ groundwater-level trends for 170,000 monitoring wells and 1,693 aquifer systems in countries that encompass approximately 75% of global groundwater withdrawals
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                    . We show that rapid groundwater-level declines (>0.5 m year
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    ) are widespread in the twenty-first century, especially in dry regions with extensive croplands. Critically, we also show that groundwater-level declines have accelerated over the past four decades in 30% of the world’s regional aquifers. This widespread acceleration in groundwater-level deepening highlights an urgent need for more effective measures to address groundwater depletion. Our analysis also reveals specific cases in which depletion trends have reversed following policy changes, managed aquifer recharge and surface-water diversions, demonstrating the potential for depleted aquifer systems to recover.
                  </jats:p>
title: Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Monitoring changes in groundwater storage (ΔGWS) is critical to assess sustainability of groundwater use under climate variability. Satellite gravimetry from the GRACE missions is used to infer ΔGWS by deducting changes in monitored or modeled water components from GRACE‐derived changes in total water storage (ΔTWS). As a residual parameter, ΔGWS is highly sensitive to arithmetic inconsistencies and uncertainties in both GRACE data and model‐derived inputs. Here we present a framework to evaluate the physical plausibility of GRACE‐derived ΔGWS estimates across 37 large global aquifer systems. The results show that the proportion of plausible ΔGWS estimates per realization, derived from multiple GRACE products and land surface model combinations, varies from <10% to >60%. Exclusion of implausible estimates improved correlations between ΔGWS and ΔTWS substantially (
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                     ≥ 0.9,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    ‐value <0.05) in most aquifers (31/37) and with in situ observations in the Bengal Basin (
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                     = 0.8,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    ‐value <0.05).
                  </jats:p>
title: Plausibility Criteria for GRACE‐Derived Groundwater Storage Changes From Aquifers Globally

items.abstract: <jats:p>Groundwater is a vital resource for direct consumption as well as for agriculture, particularly in&#160;arid and semiarid climates where groundwater is often a primary water source for irrigation.&#160;Here, we analyze more than 170,000 groundwater level timeseries across the globe.&#160;We show that groundwater level declines accelerated over the past four decades.&#160;Accelerated declines are especially widespread in dry regions with extensive cropland.&#160;However, our study also reveals that there are areas where interventions have led to groundwater&#160;levels to recover.&#160; This result provides a ray of hope for sustainable management of vital&#160;groundwater resources in the decades to come.</jats:p>
title: Accelerated Decline of Groundwater Levels in the 21st century, globally
